sections.h: Philemon: a slave sent back as a brother
sections.b: Philemon is the only New Testament writing about one enslaved person by name. Paul sends Onesimus back to his master, asks that he be received "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 1:16) and "as if he were me" (Philemon 1:17), offers to pay any debt, and says he knows Philemon will do more than he asks (Philemon 1:21). He does not say "free him." Readers have split on whether "no longer as a slave" means a new standing within the church or a hint at freedom (Lightfoot: emancipation is "trembling on his lips"). The Torah's rule, "Do not hand a slave over to his master when he has escaped from his master to you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), stands in tension with the return, though Paul's purpose is a welcome, not a punishment.

sections.h: Philemon in the American slavery debate
sections.b: Defenders of slavery read Philemon as Paul's endorsement of returning runaways. Charles Colcock Jones, preaching to enslaved people in Georgia, reported that when he condemned running away from this text, half his hearers walked out and some said there was no such letter in the Bible. Abolitionists such as Albert Barnes answered that the letter does not prove Onesimus was a slave and that its principles would end slavery. Today the Catholic Catechism cites Philemon 1:16 in teaching that enslaving people is forbidden (2414), and the Southern Baptist Convention (1995) has repudiated its founders' defense of slavery.

common: Paul does not tell Philemon in so many words to free Onesimus; whether he hints at it (1:16, 1:21) is debated.
uncommon: Onesimus was not a slave at all but Philemon's estranged brother (Allen Callahan).

claude.title: Claude's theory: "forever," but not as a slave
claude.body: The Torah's slave who chose to stay with his master would "serve him for life" (Greek: "forever"; Exodus 21:6; Deuteronomy 15:17). Paul tells Philemon he will have Onesimus back "for all time" and at once adds "no longer as a slave" (Philemon 1:15-16). The old phrase may be turned around: the man returns forever, but as a brother. This is a possible echo, not a citation.

sections.b: Colossians 3:22-4:1, sent to the same town at the same time, tells slaves to obey and masters to give their slaves what is just. Philemon shows one master being asked for far more than the code requires: to receive a returning slave as a brother, as the apostle himself, and with his debts forgiven. Readers who see the codes as accepting the social order of their day, and readers who see them as beginning to undermine it, both appeal to Philemon.

Philemon shows Paul in prison, without his title of apostle, using every art of persuasion for one man: he calls Onesimus his child, plays on his name, offers to pay his debts in a signed promise, and hopes to visit. It is the only one of his letters about a single private matter, and nearly all scholars accept it as his own.

Paul never uses the word "forgive" in Philemon, but forgiveness is what he asks for. If Onesimus has wronged Philemon or is in his debt, "put it on my account"; Paul signs the promise to repay. Christian readers from Luther on (as Lightfoot quotes him) have seen in it a picture of Christ taking the debts of others: "We are all his Onesimi."

sections.h: Welcome him as if he were me
sections.b: Philemon was a host: a church met in his house, and the saints' hearts had been "set at rest" through him (Philemon 1:2, 1:7). Paul asks him to extend that welcome to his own returning slave, "as if he were me" (Philemon 1:17), using the verb of Romans 15:7, and then asks for a guest room for himself (Philemon 1:22).

sections.h: An appeal made because of love
sections.b: Love is the key word of Philemon. Paul hears of Philemon's love for all the saints (Philemon 1:5, 1:7), appeals "because of love" instead of giving orders (Philemon 1:9), and asks him to receive Onesimus as "a much-loved brother" (Philemon 1:16). The letter shows love working on a single hard case.

Philemon is addressed to one man and also to "the church that meets in your house" (Philemon 1:2), and its greeting and blessing are plural. A private request about a slave becomes a matter for the whole congregation, in which master and slave are now brothers.

Mark, whom Paul had once refused to take along (Acts 15:37-39), is among Paul's fellow workers in Philemon 1:24, as in Colossians 4:10, and 2 Timothy 4:11 calls him useful for service, the same word Paul uses of Onesimus (Philemon 1:11).
Philemon 1:24 names Luke among Paul's fellow workers, with Demas, as Colossians 4:14 does. Only Epaphras is called Paul's "fellow captive" (Philemon 1:23).

Some scholars think Paul wrote Philemon from a prison in Ephesus, which is near Colossae and would suit his hope of a quick visit (Philemon 1:22). Acts records no imprisonment there. Some decades later, Ignatius of Antioch wrote of a bishop of Ephesus named Onesimus; John Knox argued that he was Philemon's Onesimus.

Ancient subscriptions to Philemon, and many commentators, place Paul in Rome when he wrote, during the two years of house arrest in Acts 28. Others think Rome too far from Colossae for the visit Paul hopes for (Philemon 1:22).

Philemon never uses the word "free," but readers have long asked whether "no longer as a slave" and "go beyond what I say" (Philemon 1:16, 1:21) ask Philemon to free Onesimus. Compare "But if you are able to become free, make use of it instead" (1 Corinthians 7:21).

sections.h: Philemon as a picture of substitution
sections.b: Paul's "put it on my account... I myself will repay" (Philemon 1:18-19) uses the language of accounts. Luther, as Lightfoot quotes his preface, saw in it a picture of Christ: "Even as Christ did for us with God the Father, thus also doth St Paul for Onesimus with Philemon." The letter itself is about a human debt; the picture is the readers'.

Timothy is named with Paul at the head of Philemon, "Timothy our brother" (Philemon 1:1), as in Colossians 1:1. Acts places him with Paul during the long stay at Ephesus (Acts 19:22), when Philemon may have come to know them both. The letter itself speaks in Paul's voice alone from 1:4 on.

sections.h: Why a private letter was kept
sections.b: Philemon was accepted everywhere early: Marcion kept it, Tertullian said its brevity saved it from Marcion's editing, and the Muratorian Fragment lists it. In the 300s some denied that Paul wrote it or thought it too slight for Scripture, and Jerome, Chrysostom and Theodore of Mopsuestia defended it. John Knox's theory is that Onesimus himself helped collect Paul's letters.

Colossians places Onesimus and Archippus at Colossae (Colossians 4:9; Colossians 4:17), so Philemon's house, where a church met (Philemon 1:2), is usually located there. Epaphras, the founder of the Colossian church, sends greetings in Philemon 1:23. A slave of a Colossian household, sent home "as more than a slave" (Philemon 1:16), shows the make-up of the church Colossians addresses: masters and slaves together.
